## Summary
The premise requires qualification: the sources do not establish three currently operative, compute-triggered reporting regimes. The EU has an operative compute-triggered notification duty; California has an enacted frontier-AI transparency and incident-reporting framework whose regulated class is partly defined by compute; and the U.S. federal threshold was proposed under Executive Order 14110 but lost its legal basis when that order was revoked by Executive Order 14179 in January 2025.

| Jurisdiction | Exact numeric threshold | Legal instrument and section | Effective date and current status |
|---|---:|---|---|
| **European Union** | **More than \(10^{25}\) FLOPs** of cumulative training compute. This creates a rebuttable presumption that a GPAI model has high-impact capabilities and presents systemic risk. | Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), **Arts. 51(1)(a), 51(2), and 52(1)–(2)**. Additional systemic-risk duties arise under **Art. 55**. | The Act entered into force **1 August 2024**; relevant GPAI obligations applied from **2 August 2025**. Providers must notify the Commission without delay and, in any event, within two weeks after the threshold condition is met. The Commission may also designate a model below the compute threshold based on capabilities or impact under Art. 51(1)(b). **Currently operative.** |
| **United States—federal** | **More than \(10^{26}\) FLOPs** for the principal proposed trigger; a separate proposed threshold of **\(10^{23}\) FLOPs** applied to models trained primarily on biological sequence data. | Executive Order 14110, **§4.2(a)(i) and (b)**, relying on Defense Production Act §705; implementing BIS proposed rule, **89 Fed. Reg. 73,612** (11 September 2024). | EO 14110 was issued **30 October 2023**, but did not itself make the numeric threshold operative. The BIS rule was proposed but never finalized. EO 14179, issued **23 January 2025**, revoked EO 14110. **No current operative federal threshold is established by these sources.** |
| **California** | **\(10^{26}\) FLOPs** for the statutory frontier-model line, subject to the statute’s additional model and developer-scope requirements. | California **SB-53 (2025)**, codified at **Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §§22757.11 and 22757.12**. | Effective **1 January 2026**. Section 22757.11 uses compute to define or scope the regulated frontier-AI class, while §22757.12 requires covered large developers to publish an AI framework, issue transparency reports, and confidentially report critical safety incidents to the Office of Emergency Services. The sources do **not** establish a standalone requirement to report the compute figure itself to a regulator. **Enacted and operative from the stated effective date.** |

The **EU threshold would capture the largest number of currently announced training runs**. Its \(10^{25}\)-FLOP line is one order of magnitude below the \(10^{26}\)-FLOP lines used in the proposed federal rule and California’s frontier-model framework. The available announced-run dataset reportedly identified **more than 30 models or training runs** above \(10^{25}\) FLOPs by mid-2025. Illustrative estimates include GPT-4 at approximately \(2.1\)–\(2.15\times10^{25}\) FLOPs, Llama 3.1 at roughly \(3.8\times10^{25}\), and other frontier models such as Gemini Ultra, Claude 3 Opus, Llama 3 405B, Grok 2, and Gemini 2.5 Pro.

By contrast, the sources provide no complete count of announced runs above \(10^{26}\) FLOPs. They identify examples such as Grok-3, estimated in one source at approximately \(4.6\times10^{26}\) FLOPs, and a purported GPT-4.5 run of roughly \(2\times10^{26}\) FLOPs. Thus, the proposed federal threshold and California’s numeric line would capture a much smaller subset, and California’s legal coverage would be narrower still because it depends on the statutory definitions of covered frontier models and developers.

| Numeric comparison | Approximate announced-run coverage |
|---|---|
| **EU: \(>10^{25}\) FLOPs** | Largest group; reportedly **30+** announced models/runs, based on incomplete estimates |
| **U.S. federal proposal: \(>10^{26}\) FLOPs** | Smaller subset; no reliable complete count and no current legal effect |
| **California: \(10^{26}\) FLOPs** | Numerically similar subset to the federal proposal, but subject to California’s additional developer and model-scope requirements |

The EU threshold is a presumption rather than an irrebuttable finding of risk. The Commission may designate models below it through the capability- and impact-based route, while providers may present substantiated arguments to rebut systemic-risk classification. Conversely, exceeding the threshold is not itself a measurement of actual danger; FLOPs are only a proxy for capability and may become less reliable as algorithmic efficiency improves. The Commission can adjust the EU threshold by delegated act under Article 51(3).

Providers should also distinguish the binding \(10^{25}\)-FLOP systemic-risk trigger from the separate approximate \(10^{23}\)-FLOP figure appearing in Commission guidance and commentary. That lower figure is not the AI Act’s binding notification threshold and should not be treated as an equivalent reporting mandate. Because the legal test is cumulative, providers should retain documented compute estimates across relevant training stages, including pre-training and capability-enhancing post-training where applicable, rather than assuming that splitting runs will avoid the threshold.

Accordingly, the comparison is a **threshold-based estimate, not an exact compliance count**. Training-compute figures are often undisclosed or estimated, the announced-run dataset is incomplete, and California’s framework should not be characterized as an independent compute-figure reporting regime. The U.S. federal line should be described as proposed and defunct rather than currently operative.
